This 3D asset pack was produced for CQUniversity: MMST12017 3D Computer Graphics’ Assignment 2: 3D diorama and self assessment

An oddity of the company, this one worker continues their plan of being a night owl. While everyone else has gone home, they still have their lamp on, calculator calculating, computer open, and pen writing. Unfortunately, the newton's cradle proved too distracting, so it was put to sit alongside the two dead lamps in the back area.

As usual, the coffee is still cold.

description:
One of the tests conducted at the Digital Archaeology Lab lately was to create a model of the same wooden bowl using every application that we had at our disposal, so as to have comparative data. We chose this olive wood bowl because of its patterning and its interior. This particular model was made using Trnio Plus, a photogrammetry iPad application.

Overall, we thought the little bowl was a great way to examine how these applications captured organics like wood and smaller hollowware vessels,

This vessel is in the collections of the [Petrie Museum of Egyptian Archaeology](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/culture/petrie-museum), University College London.  It is accession number UC15337.

description:
It concerns a type 2 vessel in the typology of the El Argar culture of the Siret brothers, excavated in the southeast of Spain. These hand shaped bowls with conical base come from funerary contexts, where they are often found together with type 8 vessels. This type of ceramic is characterized by a dark, polished, metallic surface. In this case the vessel had a brownish black colour. (Argaric culture, 2300 BC - 1600 BC). Inv n.: PG.41.1.086

Simple proportional editing with the sphere curve allowed me to quickly deform the flat pattern into a 'bowl' shape.

name: Ming Bowl
description:
It is unknown how or why this Chinese Ming Bowl came to be at the Family Court site in Parramatta. 
Dating from between 1400 – 1460, it may have come to Australia as an heirloom, purchased in China during the passage between Britain and Australia or represent early trade with China.

name: Dijon's Owl
description:
Located in the *rue de la Chouette* (Owl's Street), this sculpture of an owl is one of the symbols of Dijon, Burgundy, France. The custom is to pat the owl with your left hand and your wish may come true. This is why the owl lacks detail. More info on [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Notre-Dame_of_Dijon#Owl).

description: The two big new things needed to make this pin were beziar curves and spin. Firstly, the beziar curve can be draw/extruded in and then shaped with the handles. Secondly, once you have a curve, if you want to make it 3D in a sort of spherical way, then you can first convert the curve to a mesh and then spin all the vertices. Background image references, face and edge beveling, smoothe shading, sliding (GG), and subsurface division modifier were all also used in the making of this pin.

name: Mini Skyphos Cup
description: This small skyphos cup ([GR.54.1865](https://data.fitzmuseum.cam.ac.uk/id/object/65806)) was found at a classical cemetery at Kranioi in Cephalonia, a Greek Island near Corinth, Greece and dates from 500 B.C. — 401 B.C. A skyphos is a deep-bowled drinking vessel with a low foot and two short handles, and these minature versions are found in Corinthian pottery production during this period. These cups are often found at sanctuaries, suggesting their use as votive offerings throughout the region.

name: Wormhole, Peniche
description: Dissolved calcareous rock, Peniche, Portugal. Wormholes are dissolution features forming slowly during flow in joints: slightly acidic water dissolves calcites. In proper conditions of fast enough flow in fine enough initially quasiplanar open fractures (joints), cylindrical-like channels develop, carving the planar boundaries. These features, related to a natural instability, are known as wormholes.

In combat, after arming, the grenade was thrown on top of the slowly advancing tank where the armor was thin.

name: Example recessive inheritance 一
description:
Orange the unaffected gene
Blue the affected gene
Both parents must pass on an affected gene for a chance of getting albinism in this case. That's what you call it recessive inheritance.

One parent (no albinism) the other parent (does have albinism). They have 4 children. They all have the albinism gene and can pass on the albinism gene again, but they don't have albinism.
All children are carriers of the albinism gene.
